questions.problem: Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2{e}^{3\theta }$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2{e}^{3\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=6{e}^{3\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{3\theta })}^{2}+{(6{e}^{3\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{e}^{6\theta }+36{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{40{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{10}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{e}^{3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3}{e}^{3\theta }{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3}({e}^{3\pi /2}-{e}^{-3\pi /2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{({\theta }^{2}+2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2(\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+2}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}+(12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+144{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{2\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2{e}^{2\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{2\theta })}^{2}+{(2{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{4\theta }+4{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{[{e}^{2\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{2(\pi /2)}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$
